Welcome! This newsletter brings together two projects rethinking the deep-time evolution of human technology. <strong><a href="https://zoogestures.uni-koeln.de/" class="zoogestures-name">ZOOGESTURES</a></strong> explores the overlooked role of nonhuman animal gestures in inspiring and scaffolding technical learning and innovation in early human evolution. <strong><a href="https://ecolithic.uni-koeln.de/" class="ecolithic-name">ECOLITHIC</a></strong> develops a radical new ecosystems view of long-term Palaeolithic stone tool evolution. Together, they open up fresh perspectives on how humans became technological beings – never alone, but always in relation to their wider world!

<br>


<div class="ecolithic">


# ECOLITHIC: A Radical Ecosystems View of Lithic Macro-Evolution

<strong><a href="https://ecolithic.uni-koeln.de/" class="ecolithic-name">ECOLITHIC</a></strong> is the acronym for “A Radical Ecosystems View of Lithic Macro-Evolution”. It is a new 3-year, interdisciplinary project generously funded through the [VolkswagenFoundation’s “Pioneering Research – Exploring the Unknown Unknown” funding line](https://www.volkswagenstiftung.de/en/funding/funding-offer/pioneering-research-exploring-unknown-unknown). In the project, archaeologists, environmental humanities scholars, philosophers of technology, evolutionary theorists, paleontologists as well as Earth system, complexity, and network scientists work together to develop novel perspectives on long-term technological change in the human deep past, roughly spanning the timeframe between 120,000 and 15,000 years ago in Europe, the periods archaeologists describe as Middle and Upper Palaeolithic. Inspired by the proliferation of “planetary” thinking and the undertheorized scalability of technology, ECOLITHIC aims to explore the organisational properties of higher-order technological worlds. It proposes that a true macro-archaeology of long-term evolution in early technologies such as stone artefact production and use needs to pay closer attention to how different technical systems assemble, interact, and become integrated in broader ecosystems of technical action and knowledge.


## Happenings


<div class="news-item">

### **Anaïs L. Vignoles joins ECOLITHIC** (January 1)

Anaïs L. Vignoles joins the University of Cologne and the ECOLITHIC project as a postdoctoral researcher, supporting the team for the next 2 years. She is a prehistoric archaeologist interested in lithic technological evolution, the dynamic interaction of material culture and climate on evolutionary time scales, and the relationship between ecological and technological diversity. In the project, she explores how technical systems coexist in the Late Middle and Upper Palaeolithic of southwestern France, with a focus on Gravettian blade and bladelet technology.

### **First ECOLITHIC Workshop in Cologne** (April 21–23)

Anaïs L. Vignoles and Shumon T. Hussain hosted a 4-day international workshop with the external project collaborators to discuss interdisciplinary perspectives on long-term macroevolution and to develop a new research framework for studying it in and testing it against the Pleistocene archaeological record. Using the facilities of MESH and the Department for Prehistoric Archaeology, we discussed higher-level system properties (Hussain), synergy (Vignoles), hierarchical organisation (Temkin), scaling and scale-dependency (Spiridonov), collaborative decision-making (Barfuss), invention and evolvability (Charbonneau), relational network thinking including hypergraphs (Valverde), and technological enactivism (Feiten).

<div class="zoogestures">

# ZOOGESTURES - Interspecies Learning and Technical Invention in Early Human Evolution

<strong><a href="https://zoogestures.uni-koeln.de/" class="zoogestures-name">ZOOGESTURES</a></strong> is the acronym for “The Zoomorphology of Gestures: Interspecies Learning and Technical Invention in Early Human Evolution”. It is a 4-year, collaborative and cross-university project integrating archaeological (Cologne), philosophical and anthropological (Siegen), as well as primatological (St Andrews) lines of inquiry into human and nonhuman gestural and technical behaviour to develop a novel research programme to better understand how humans and nonhumans may have inspired and learnt from each other over evolutionary timescales. Generously funded through the [VolkswagenFoundation’s “Pioneering Research – Exploring the Unknown Unknown” funding line](https://www.volkswagenstiftung.de/en/funding/funding-offer/pioneering-research-exploring-unknown-unknown), ZOOGESTURES combines theory-work, cross-period synthesis and comparison, as well as fieldwork in Africa (and possibly elsewhere) to explore the significance of cross-species cohabitation and interaction for the evolution of behavioural novelty, in particular the hitherto overlooked role of other animals in processes of human technical invention.

## Happenings

<div class="news-item">
### **Matthew Henderson joins ZOOGESTURES** (March 1)

[Matthew joins ZOOGESTURES](https://zoogestures.uni-koeln.de/people/matthew-henderson) as a postdoctoral researcher and comparative psychologist, with a background of behavioural primatology and gestural communication. His PhD explored how the ‘human-ape’ retains access to a shared ape-typical gestural repertoire, and how this bodily communication system has scaffolded for the emergence of language. For the ZOOGESTURES project, he brings his experience of human and nonhuman ape research across varied environments to help explore the influence that cross-species learning has had (and still has) across hominids.

</div>

<div class="news-item">

### **Rebekka I.I. Eckelmann joins ZOOGESTURES** (June 1)

[Rebekka joins ZOOGESTURES](https://zoogestures.uni-koeln.de/people/rebekka-ii-eckelmann) as a postdoctoral researcher and multispecies archaeologist, with a background in faunal osteology and isotope biogeochemistry. Her research explores how human–nonhuman relationships shaped past subsistence, social organisation and technological practices. Within ZOOGESTURES, she brings an archaeological perspective to past socio-zoo-technical relations.
</div>

<div class="news-item">
### **Welcome to the team, Rebekka and Matthew!**
</div>

<div class="news-item">
### **ZOOGESTURES kicks off with a Bang – Launch at the Department for Prehistoric Archaeology (Cologne) attracts diverse audience** (July 15)

![ZOOGESTURES Kick Start event starting in Cologne here with Johannes, Shumon, Bar, and Rebekka (left to right).](ZG_Starter.jpeg)

On 15 July, ZOOGESTURES celebrated its official launch, with Multispecies Archaeology (Cologne) now active as the last of the three work packages, following the start of work in Philosophy of Technology (Siegen) and Primatology (St Andrews) earlier this year. The Kick-Start Event brought together more than 20 participants from Prehistoric Archaeology, MESH, Philosophy, African Studies and beyond for an afternoon of presentations, discussion and exchange.

Following an introduction to the project by Shumon T. Hussain and Rebekka I.I. Eckelmann, the programme continued with contributions from Thomas Widlok, who explored the distinction between technique as transfer and technique as culture, and Johannes Schick, who spoke on containers, media and multispecies technology in early evolution. We were particularly pleased to welcome external speakers Sonja Tomasso (Liege), who offered a functional-analytical perspective on animal materials in stone-tool technology, and Bar Efrati (Oxford), with a theoretical exploration of the “multispecies chaîne opératoire”.

What really stood out was the lively discussion in between, full of probing questions and unexpected connections. ZOOGESTURES’ core idea – that human technology has never been a purely human affair – clearly resonated beyond our own disciplinary boundaries, opening up possibilities for new collaborations.

</div>

## Meeting the Team

<div class="news-item">
### Today: [Johannes Schick](https://zoogestures.uni-koeln.de/people/johannes-f-m-schick)

![Andreas Hüttemann (Vice Dean, Faculty of Arts and Humanities) congratulating Johannes at  his habilitation lecture.](J_lecture.jpg)


**1. What is your role in ZOOGESTURES, and how does it connect to the project's major objectives?**

I understand my role as “interdisciplinary anthropologist”, i.e, I attempt to operate in between the disciplines to draw conclusions from the empirical research for a theoretical, techno-anthropological framework. So I hope to develop a theory that accounts for the invention of technical gestures as multispecies event. This would in turn also allow to shed new light on archaeological and primatological findings.

**2. How does your past or ongoing research feed into the project and shape its interdisciplinary perspective?**

Well, I have been working for a long time on questions of how to conceive of an interdisciplinary anthropology and of how the categories of the human mind are generated. The project provides an opportunity to test my theory and to apply it to multispecies studies. I hope that my focus on practices and processes also co-shapes how we approach our work as a team.

**3. What are you working on at the moment, and what is especially exciting about it?**

At the moment I work on Simondon’s concept of the “associated milieu” as a condition of possibility for multispecies technical gestures. It allows me to push the limits of the concept and see if it fits to the phenomena and findings from archeology and primatology.

**4. What's one surprising insight you've had while working on this research?**

I am constantly surprised by the abilities of animals. So far, all the empirical examples of multispecies co-habitation, co-evolution and co-culture have been surprising. Just now, I read how sika deer and macaques form social relations with each other.


**Johannes Schick delivered his habilitation lecture “„Wir hätten nur noch einen Technologen gebraucht, um vollständig zu sein“ (Marcel Mauss) – Über den Versuch einer interdisziplinären Technikanthropologie“ [„"All we needed was a technologist to be complete" (Marcel Mauss) - On the attempt to develop an interdisciplinary anthropology of technology] on the 1st of June.**

**Many congratulations from the team!**

</div>

## From the Labs - Ongoing Work
<div class="news-item">

- The ZOOGESTURES team is currently planning the 1st project workshop to be held in Cologne in November 2026 and its joint primatological-anthropological fieldwork programme, starting in 2027.

- Cat has had a great summer of fieldwork thinking about ZOOGESTURES themed ideas! She and the Wild Minds Lab continue their work on sacred baboons, with communities who take primates as totems with anthropomorphic characteristics and a number of elephant-based projects, including on the question ‘what it means to be an elephant’ with Peter Butler-way. Wild Minds also started a collaboration with Dr Elodie Freymann on a Rights of Nature approach to networks of medicinal plant use that erode traditional boundaries around species-specific knowledge.

- Johannes is currently working on Simondon’s concept of the “associated milieu” as a condition of possibility for multispecies technical gestures. Furthermore, he is researching how the genesis of the categories of human understanding is co-constituted by multi-species relations and whether or not containers as fundamental technologies can also be considered as ZOOGESTURES.

- Matthew has been investigating examples of medicinal practices of nonhuman animals and reports of which of these have been adopted by humans. The aim is to improve our understanding of of general biases in what humans pay attention to when it comes to nonhuman species (mostly focussing on relatedness and proximity biases). So far, he collected 186 cases of animal medicinal behaviour across 141 taxa, testing relatedness and proximity as explanations for which practices crossed into human use. He has also been working on making new software tools to help code audio/video data and to run/share experiments easily in remote fieldwork conditions. This includes a bioacoustics software focused on coding bioacoustics data (onset timing, rhythm metrics, linking audio to video) for the initial Environmental Landscape Rhythm project exploring cross-species rhythmic alignment between (e.g., chimpanzee drumming, bird song, human soundscapes) with the hope to extend it into other kinds of data coding as well. A second software is an offline, cross-platform experiment running app with a full experiment builder, any-language or icon-only interfaces and basic on-device gaze tracking/gyro tracking. He has already rebuilt the Wild Minds Lab’s completed ‘Great Ape Dictionary’ study that was originally run on gorilla.sc (which requires persistent online connection to work) which can be shared with communities of people who have differing moral/ethical concerns for chimpanzees to understand the role this plays in understanding communicative behaviours in these species.


- Rebekka is exploring how animals could have shaped technological learning, beginning with enigmatic marine animals as a first area of investigation. Alongside this, she and colleagues are working with the role of hares and multispecies learning in two Neolithic contexts.


</div>

</div>
